Honda Auto Stop-Start Issue Prompts NHTSA Investigation, 1 Million Vehicles Potentially Affected
23 photos
Photo: Honda
The safety boffins at the Office of Safety Investigations have opened an engineering analysis into American Honda Motor vehicles with automatic start-stop systems that may not work as intended. More specifically, these systems may fail to restart the engine automatically from a complete stop.
Said investigation covers a whopping 1,033,632 automobiles produced for model years 2024 through 2026. Meanwhile, the latest American Honda Motor service documentation instructs owners to disable the system while the manufacturer deals with limited replacement parts availability.
EA26007 covers the Odyssey minivan, Passport and Pilot crossovers, and the Ridgeline pickup, together with the Pilot-twinned Acura MDX. The federal agency has collected 701 complaints as of this writing, alleging that the engine doesn't restart automatically after the driver releases the brake pedal. Keeping the engine off when the traffic light turns green or when the driver wants to make a turn at an intersection definitely sounds like a safety risk.
Per service bulletin 26-090, vehicles may also experience a slow crank or fail to start under hot ambient temperature conditions. Published by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on October 30, 2026, the bulletin states that repairs are available only for vehicles experiencing symptoms. American Honda Motor blames limited parts availability.
1-888-234-2138 is the customer support and campaign center number customers can call for additional information. The bulletin covers 2020 through 2026 Odyssey models, the 2018 to 2019 Odyssey Touring and Elite, 2019 through 2025 Passport models, the 2016 to 2022 Pilot, and the 2020 to 2026 Ridgeline. Customers are further advised to check their VINs to establish eligibility.
Photo: Honda Acura doesn't appear in the cited service bulletin, and the bulletin does not explain which parts are being replaced. Once sufficient replacement parts become available, Honda plans another notification. More curious still, the saga kicked off years ago, back in June 2022. It all started with PE22005, a preliminary evaluation prompted by complaints about the Auto Idle Stop system in older Pilots.
The NHTSA's ODI subsequently expanded the examination, elevating it to an engineering analysis in March 2025. EA25004 covered a simply ludicrous 2,209,466 vehicles, including the TLX sedan. Its opening report highlighted 1,348 complaints, four crash incidents, and two injuries, and the NHTSA also learned about owners who needed a jump-start before they could continue driving.
Countermeasures were introduced in January 2023 through service bulletins 23-008 and 23-009. If updating the fuel injection software failed to fix things, authorized dealers were required to replace the starter assembly, relay, and adjust the valves. In addition, American Honda Motor extended warranty coverage to 10 years with unlimited mileage for vehicles that needed replacement parts.
The complaints, however, continued after these corrective actions. Per the NHTSA, many owners claim that dealers had already completed the prescribed countermeasures on their vehicles. Adding to the confusion, EA26007 reads that vehicles involved in the current investigation appear to have different root causes for their auto start-stop woes. They also appear to respond differently to repairs.
Being an engineering analysis, EA26007 aims to establish the potential safety risks, severity, and scope of the problem. At the same time, Honda Motor America needs to establish why newer vehicles apparently require a different approach from those involved in the earlier investigation.

Most SUVs are lucky to tow a small trailer without breaking a sweat. BYD’s new luxury SUV had a slightly bigger challenge: pulling a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet. And somehow, it did it on just two wheels. The video is worth a look.
BYD Denza Bao 5 vs jumbo jet, on two wheels
The Bao 5 made its European debut at the Goodwood Festival of Speed (FOS) in July, the first SUV from BYD’s “premium technology-focused” brand, Denza.
As Denza’s first SUV designed specifically for Europe, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, said the company is “confident that the Bao 5 will be a huge hit,” offering the perfect mix of off-road ability, luxury, and advanced technology.
The SUV uses BYD’s DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) plug-in hybrid powertrain, which BYD said is the “world’s first off-road-dedicated hybrid architecture/”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
BYD’s off-road PHEV powertrain features three electric motors (one on each axle and a third generator) and a 1.5L turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 536 horsepower (544 PS) and 560 lb-ft (760 Nm) of torque.
BYD boasted that “Those figures – well clear of PHEV rivals’ and comfortably more than conventional diesel SUVs’ – are enough for a 0-100km/h time of just 4.8 seconds.”
BYD Denza Bao 5 SUV pulls a Boeing 747 jumbo jet on two wheels (Source: Denza)
To top it off, BYD added a double wishbone front and rear suspension with its DiSus-P intelligent body system, plus front and rear intelligent electronic differential locks with millisecond-level response to improve traction and performance.
The Bao 5 is equipped with a 31.8 kWh BYD Blade Battery that delivers a pure-electric WLTP range of up to 56 miles (90 km). And on a full tank and a full charge, the WLTP combined range is 537 miles (835 km).
To prove the new luxury SUV’s capabilities, BYD put it to the ultimate test — towing a Boeing 747 jumbo jet using just two wheels.
BYD Denza Bao 5 SUV pulls a Boeing 747 jumbo jet on two wheels (Source: Denza)
While pulling a 180-tonne, or nearly 400,000-pound, jumbo jet on four wheels is impressive in itself, Denza’s engineers wanted to push it further, doing something never tried before to showcase its off-road DMO technology.
The Bao 5 was put to the test at Dunsfold Aerodrome airfield in Surrey, England. It successfully pulled the jumbo jet in each of its three runs: one on four wheels, one on three, and the last on just two wheels.
Combined, the SUV towed the 747 for a total of 1,600 meters, or close to a mile, which BYD said is about four laps around a standard-size athletic track.

SEAT Brand Could Be Phased Out as Cupra Prepares for Electric-Only Switchover
21 photos
Photo: Cupra
Even though Cupra wants to get rid of internal combustion at some point in the future, it simply does not know when. The problem with this outlook is that Cupra's best-selling model as of this writing is the Formentor, a compact-sized crossover that can be had with 1.5- to 2.5-liter mills. Indeed, the range-topping VZ5 specification uses the Audi turbocharged five-pot mill we all know and love.
At the same time, the SEAT brand is still trying to convince the Volkswagen Group that more affordable vehicles deserve another generation. Markus Haupt, who runs both of them, made his intentions clear at the Automobilwoche Congress in Berlin. As reported by Automotive News, the cooler marque with the pricier models is described by Haupt as the Spanish operation's growth engine.
The big kahuna also said that customer demand will dictate the switchover to electric-only models for Cupra , which is unbelievably vague. Adding insult to injury, the European Union has moved to replace its 2035 zero-emission mandate with a much softer fleet CO2 reduction target. Under the new arrangement, internal combustion and hybrid vehicles will remain on sale past 2035.
If you ask me, it's totally unsurprising how Cupra is now open to internal combustion vehicles for as long as there is demand for them. Automotive executives have spent years announcing electrification deadlines, only to discover that blindly following legislators doesn't automatically mean increased demand for electric vehicles in Spain and other European markets.
Cupra, meanwhile, depends heavily on combustion vehicles while its full-electric lineup matures. Cupra recorded nearly 224,000 registrations in Europe between January 2026 and September 2026, putting it well ahead of SEAT's 155,777-vehicle tally.
That's 44 percent in Cupra's favor, and the suits in Wolfsburg are right to get behind Cupra. They're not right in assuming that its growth means that SEAT may have to go.
Photo: Cupra It's been a few years since we first heard that SEAT may become an urban mobility brand or get discontinued altogether. The only certain thing we are currently aware of is that SEAT's current roadmap ends in 2029. Following the introduction of mild-hybrid variants for the Ibiza and Arona in 2027, the company outlined plans for a full-hybrid Leon in 2028. Come 2029, a bigger redesign may be on the menu.
Nothing has been publicly decided after 2029, though, and this is the reason why enthusiasts believe that Volkswagen is phasing out SEAT after its current products reach the end of their production life cycles. Martorell will remain busy regardless of what happens to said badge.
The Martorell plant has taken responsibility for production of the group's Electric Urban Car Family, which comprises four members: the Cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo hatchbacks on one hand, plus the Skoda Epiq and the Volkswagen ID. Cross front-drive crossovers on the other.
As opposed to a starting price of 16,900 euros in Spain for the internal combustion Polo, the zero-emission sibling is advertised at 17,900 euros from the outset, making it an interesting B-segment electric vehicle. The ID. Cross, meanwhile, slots between the T-Cross and Taigo in terms of pricing.
20,500 euros puts the ID. Cross higher than the Epiq, which is 18,500 euros for the most basic specification available in Spain. The Raval is the most expensive of the bunch in base flavor, with the Plus grade retailing at 28,610 euros in Spain.

Man Blows Over $100K on New HEMI-Powered Jeep Wrangler in 2026, Sells for $70K After 6,700 Miles
14 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
A couple of years ago, Jeep announced that it will pull the plug on the Wrangler 392 with the aptly-called Final Edition , though due to customer demand and shifting electrification plans, the company decided to keep it in its lineup.
Therefore, those who want a V8-powered Wrangler can buy one directly from Jeep’s official dealer network, and the offering includes the Willys 392 and the Moab 392 for the 2027 model year, which have MSRPs of $70,995 and $79,995, respectively. Or they could search the used car market for one, and that is where we found the example pictured above.
It is a 2025 model year Jeep Wrangler Unlimited Rubicon 392 Final Edition 4x4 , which was picked up by the seller new in April 2026. The man added a little over 6,700 miles (~10,800 km) before deciding to part ways with his SUV for unknown reasons, and he advertised it on Cars&Bids, When the gavel hit the table on November 17, 2026, the vehicle changed hands for $70,199, thus leaving a toll on the seller’s finances.
That’s because the man paid $107,575 for his V8-powered Jeep Wrangler a little over half a year ago, so he lost $37,376 in just seven months. Thus, the ride ended up costing him over $5.5 per mile, excluding the gasoline and other work that he might have poured into it.
Photo: Cars&Bids This Jeep Wrangler is finished in Granite Crystal Metallic Clear Coat, has a black interior, and a clean Florida title. It has never been involved in an accident, and comes with the Customer Preferred Package 27J, Heavy Duty Full Flooring System, Off-Road Plus mode, Tru-Lok front and rear axles, and Sky One-Touch power top.
Moreover, it also features quarter window storage bags, heavy-duty rock sliders with step assist, a transfer skid plate, removable quarter windows, power-adjustable and heated front seats, a 12.3-inch touchscreen display (Uconnect5), and an Alpine sound system.
There are no flaws mentioned in the listing, which reveals that the engine oil and filter were changed in September 2026, at 4,952 miles (7,969 km), and that the vehicle is accompanied by two keys, the owner’s manual, and the window sticker.
Power comes from a 6.4-liter HEMI V8 , making 470 hp (477 ps/350 kW) and 470 lb-ft (637 Nm) of torque, which drives all four wheels through an 8-speed automatic transmission, and a 2-speed transfer case.
This was definitely a great deal for the new owner, who got an almost-new V8-powered Wrangler that features a lot of extras for almost $40K less. Rivian’s new electric bike spinoff, ALSO, has hit another speed bump. The company has announced that it is temporarily halting deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycles after discovering software-related problems affecting some bikes, including issues with charging behavior.
And unfortunately, this isn’t entirely surprising. We’ve already reported on some strange battery behavior with the new e-bikes, as well as customers having to send their bikes back for repairs.
In a message sent to customers, ALSO explained that it was pausing shipments to address several software problems before more bikes reach riders.
“We’ve identified a few software-based issues, such as charging behavior, that are impacting some bikes,” the company explained.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
ALSO says its engineers are working on a firmware update to resolve the problems, with shipments expected to resume in approximately two weeks.
The pause affects the remaining Launch Edition deliveries as well as the beginning of Performance Edition shipments, both of which will now arrive later than previously promised.
We saw some of these problems coming
The announcement follows earlier reports of unusual charging and discharging behavior on the TM-B, which we previously highlighted as some of the growing pains facing Rivian’s ambitious new e-bike venture.
We’ve also reported on customers needing to return their bikes for repairs, raising questions about how smoothly the company’s initial rollout was progressing.
The issues align with many of our initial concerns we discussed a year ago when the bike was first unveiled, namely that the high-tech design means the bike incorporates many new and proprietary systems that could each lead to complicated and costly failures.
Now ALSO has officially acknowledged software problems affecting some bikes, including charging behavior, though it hasn’t detailed the full extent of the issues or confirmed whether they are directly related to those earlier reports.
The bike represents a fairly radical departure from traditional electric bicycles, with proprietary technology throughout its drivetrain and control systems. That makes software an especially important part of the ownership experience.
To ALSO’s credit, pausing deliveries to fix known problems is probably the right move. Nobody wants to receive a premium-priced electric bicycle only to discover that it needs an immediate trip back to the manufacturer.
But for customers who have already waited longer than expected, another delay is undoubtedly frustrating.
ALSO says it will provide another update on November 24, hopefully with better news about when deliveries can resume.

source_document.body:
The sheer scale of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers dominates the conversation about their power needs. But the way these facilities draw electricity may be the harder problem for utilities and on-site generators to solve. That is the view of Brad Witter, senior vice president of Industrial Digital at Generac, who discussed the issue on The POWER Podcast .
Witter said the industry’s answer is increasingly energy storage: batteries and fast-acting inverters that sit between the load and the grid, smoothing demand and riding through faults. Proving that those systems will work together at utility scale, he added, will depend as much on simulation as on hardware.
Three Problems, Not One
Witter described the challenge in three parts: magnitude, spikiness, and fault intolerance. On magnitude, he pointed to a data center proposed in Utah that he said equals the entire state’s load.
Size alone does not capture the risk, however. AI training clusters, in which thousands of GPUs (graphics processing units) work on a single model, change state together, Witter said. When a step finishes or an interruption occurs, “they all interrupt at once.” In a traditional data center, nodes work more independently, so their ups and downs offset one another and the overall load stays flatter. In an AI cluster, he said, “when one goes up, they all go up.”
That behavior is difficult for a grid built around stable, predictable load patterns. Witter offered the example of the largest load on a distribution feeder swinging up and down 50% at the millisecond level. “The spikiness is every bit as much of a problem as the magnitude is,” he said.
The third problem is fault response. Witter said these facilities are very sensitive to power quality, and many drop offline automatically when the grid struggles, which makes a bad situation worse for the utility. Generation behind the meter is not spared, he added. All of that spinning generation “does not like that spikiness,” he said, and turbines in particular can be damaged by repeated swings of that size.
Utilities Set the Terms
Developers want to go faster and utilities want to go slower, Witter said, because a utility cannot add that much capacity to an already strained system on short notice. The practical result, he said, is that many utilities are asking large loads for two things. The first is to bring their own generation, such as turbines or fuel cells, to bridge the gap while the utility catches up. The second is to behave differently once connected, limiting both the spikiness of their demand and their response to grid faults.
Asked whether utilities are in the driver’s seat, Witter said, “I would cautiously say yes,” noting that community benefits and revenue also give utilities reasons to move quickly. He said he expects hyperscalers to take on a larger share of the required investment in future interconnection agreements, and that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) is getting involved. He described hyperscalers’ willingness to build their own natural gas power plants as a bridge as unprecedented, and characterized the current market as “a land grab.”
Batteries as the Buffer
The scale of conventional backup alone is substantial, Witter said. A 200-MW site, he noted, could require hundreds of generators. To meet utility requirements and still protect on-site equipment, he said, facilities need a buffer in the form of energy storage, which flattens load swings and provides ride-through support during faults. He described storage as almost a necessity for some utility requirements, “table stakes” for securing an interconnection agreement.
Witter expects that buffer to come from two directions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) providers, whose batteries protect power at the rack, are moving their capabilities closer to the meter, he said, though he noted that rack-level UPS systems do not help with load smoothing or grid stability. Standalone battery energy storage, meanwhile, can serve as what he called a facility-level UPS.
Grid-forming inverters are what deliver that buffer, Witter said. Connected in parallel with the load, they can charge when demand dips and discharge when it rises, offsetting the swings. Because they can form a local grid without the utility present, they can also black start a site. Automation then decides when generators need to run. That arrangement, he said, makes the battery system “the central nervous system” of a site’s off-grid support.
Proving It Before Building It
Validating these architectures is its own challenge. “You can’t do a proof of concept with a half a gigawatt of infrastructure,” Witter said, and no one will fund a multibillion-dollar test case. Manufacturers must show that equipment meets specifications on paper, he said, but how the pieces interact is “way more important” than whether each one complies individually. Utility-scale simulation, he said, is the only way to build confidence before committing at full scale.
Witter said labs such as the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly the National Renewable Energy Laboratory [NREL]) are partnering with manufacturers on hybrid testing that mixes real hardware with simulation, and that Generac has an ongoing effort with the lab. He added that utilities now commonly require modeling evidence in interconnection submissions, showing how a facility’s systems would respond to specified grid disturbances.
That integration challenge also shapes Generac’s strategy, according to Witter. He said the company has added switchgear, packaging, and transfer switch capabilities and is investing heavily in battery storage, because customers increasingly want a single partner and the orchestration involved is far more complex than the “couple wires” that traditionally tie backup power together. He said Generac’s architecture remains open to third-party equipment.
AI itself is part of the answer, Witter added. He said Generac uses it for predictive failure algorithms and manufacturing quality, and that large language models may speed the simulation work needed to prove these systems. He called it “an ironic circular loop,” with AI creating the problem it will help solve.
What Success Looks Like
Looking five years out, Witter said the data centers that got their power strategy right will be the ones that got online at all. Reaching an actionable agreement with the utility is among the biggest hurdles, he said, and many of the technologies involved are not yet fully proven. “The ones that get it right are the ones that work,” he said.
For developers that must build bridging power now, he said, the greatest benefit will go to those who plan how that equipment will support the site once utility power arrives, so nothing has to be ripped out and replaced.

GM Looks Outside Its Ranks for Mary Barra's Replacement as CEO
8 photos
Photo: GM
Mary Barra has spent a good part of her working life at General Motors. The 64-year-old chief executive officer climbed from a cooperative education job at Pontiac while earning her electrical engineering degree to the corner office of America's largest automaker, but now, General Motors is looking beyond its ranks to identify possible successors.
Even though candidates from within are considered, the Wall Street Journal reports that General Motors hired an outside executive search firm to examine potential external candidates. According to people familiar with the matter, internal contenders include finance chief Paul Jacobson, chief product officer Sterling Anderson, and prez Mark Reuss.
Reuss is best viewed as Barra's second-in-command at General Motors . The automaker has obviously declined to comment on this matter, and the WSJ report does not mention when Barra might leave. Reading between the lines, this is nothing more than succession planning rather than a resignation announcement in the making.
It is worth noting that Mary recently stated that she feels energized in her current role, adding that she'd like to continue leading the company. Even so, the WSJ's information lays the groundwork for a transition. The search for outsiders is a bit curious for General Motors, which has historically promoted its own execs to the CEO role.
On this occasion, whoever comes next will inherit an automaker facing competing demands from its expensive electrification programs, autonomous driving ambitions, and formidable Chinese rivals. Following her co-op at the Pontiac division, Barra earned her MBA from the Stanford Graduate School of Business through a GM fellowship program.
Photo: GM Mary's career at GM took her through engineering positions, the Detroit-Hamtramck assembly plant that is now called Factory Zero, global manufacturing engineering, and even human resources. Barra eventually moved into product development. Back in 2011, she became senior vice prez of global product development. By 2023, her responsibilities further included purchasing and supply chain.
Barra held the executive VP role when the board of directors selected her as Dan Akerson's replacement. The appointment was announced in December 2013, with Mary taking over in January 2014. She became the first woman to lead a major global automaker, and frankly speaking, Mary couldn't have taken her position at a worse time.
Back in February 2014, the ignition switch recall saga kicked off with the Chevrolet Cobalt and many other models fitted with shorter-than-required detent plungers. Due to insufficient torque resistance, the ignition switch could move out of the run position into accessory mode or off, increasing the risk of a crash. In off, the airbags are disabled as well, leaving occupants without adequate protection.
Barra may have inherited that mess, but she masterfully answered for it as chief executive officer, with General Motors dismissing 15 employees in the process. Over the years, Mary owned GM products that include the fifth-gen Camaro (SS) and the seventh-generation Corvette (Z06 with the Z07 package).
Under Barra's tenure, General Motors also retreated from several unprofitable international markets while the company also reduced its global vehicle portfolio. While the company may sell millions fewer vehicles worldwide than it did a decade ago, shares have climbed more than 130 percent since Mary took over.
Whoever follows Mary will inherit a lucrative US truck operation that generates the money needed to fund next-gen products, including a bunch of large hybrid sport utility vehicles . Even so, the newcomer still has to make decisions affecting the automaker's electrification and autonomous driving businesses.

Truckload carriers that can’t dispatch a truck for a tendered load now have somewhere to send it besides back to the shipper. Graypool , the Atlanta freight software company formerly known as HOPTEK, opened Graypool Exchange on Wednesday. It launched with seven founding member carriers, which pass qualified freight directly to one another.
The exchange runs inside the tender software Graypool already operates for its carriers. When a member can’t put a truck on a load it wants to keep, the system can offer that load to other members before the carrier rejects it. Each member sets which freight it will offer, which it will take, and at what price.
The launch comes as carriers turn away far more contract freight than a year ago. Third-quarter tender rejections averaged 14.5%, up from 5.3% a year earlier, according to the SONAR Truckload Rejection Index . Rejections have since eased to 12.77% in the index’s latest weekly reading, the lowest since early May.
“Across the U.S., truckload carriers turn away freight they want every day, not because the lane is wrong, but because the truck is,” Graypool CEO Marc Held said in the release. “Until now, carriers have had no venue of their own to send it to.”
What happens to a rejected tender today
When a carrier rejects a tender, the shipper offers the load to the next carrier in its routing guide . Each step down that list costs more. Shippers paid 9.25% more for loads accepted on the second tender, according to SONAR’s Routing Guide Premiums index when it launched in late October. Loads that slid to the third tender or beyond cost 19.84% more.
The exchange gives the first carrier another option, Held said in an interview with FreightWaves. A shipper offers Carrier A a load at $100. If Carrier A has no truck in position but Carrier B will run it for $80, Carrier A keeps the shipper and $20 of margin . Carrier B gets freight it could not otherwise reach.
“It gives them the ability to always say yes, because the one thing that a carrier always wants to do is when someone says, ‘Hey, will you move this from point A to point B?’ They always want to say yes. Period,” Held said. “The thing that we are just enabling them to do is making it so that they can say yes profitably.”
Seven members, by invitation only
The exchange is open to carriers by invitation. Members operate under shared commercial, data, and insurance standards, with interchange agreements approved by their insurers, according to the release. Only loads whose shippers allow a hand-off reach the exchange. Freight a shipper requires its contracted carrier to run never gets there.
Graypool runs the exchange, holds no freight of its own, and takes no side in a trade. “We don’t take the load. We don’t broker it. We run the floor,” Held said in the release.
Because Graypool already decides which loads fit each carrier’s network, the system can ask every member at once whether it wants a load, Held said. The answer has to come back in under five seconds.
“There is no separate load board where a carrier needs to bid on these assets again,” he said. “We’re already doing that.”
Paper Transport, a Graypool customer, backed the exchange in the release. “Graypool Exchange is our first choice for finding capacity we can trust and freight from respected partners,” said Ben Schill, corporate development officer at Paper Transport.
Graypool’s existing carrier business
The exchange is Graypool’s third product. Graypool Accept decides which tendered freight enters a carrier’s network, and Graypool Source finds and bids on spot freight . Graypool said carriers have booked $150 million in annualized freight revenue through Source.
Graypool’s customers include Werner, Marten, Prime, Hirschbach, Paper Transport, and Maybach International Group. The company raised $5 million in pre-seed funding from Jerk Ventures, Kearney, LPX Partners, Venture 53, and Werner Enterprises when it dropped the HOPTEK name in October.
But the exchange starts small. Shippers do not send freight to it directly, Held said. It works off the contract tenders and spot loads Graypool already handles for its carriers.
Held compares Graypool to exchange operators such as Nasdaq and Intercontinental Exchange. “I think the magic is in actually turning these over-the-counter marketplaces into a single clearing house,” he said.
Why it matters: Asset carriers bidding on 2027 contract freight can commit to lanes their own trucks won’t always reach, provided other members cover the gaps. That math gets sharper if rejections hold above 12% through January, which a FreightWaves SONAR analysis says would make double-digit contract increases the base case.

Werner has spent years building its answer. The company has a long record of hiring veterans and has repeatedly been recognized as a top military-friendly employer. We spoke with Greg Hamm, Vice President of Government and Field Recruiting at Werner, about how that effort works today, why team driving has become a central piece of it and what a veteran can expect from the first day of orientation to a permanent truck.
A pipeline, not a campaign
Plenty of carriers run a Veterans Day promotion and call it a military strategy. Hamm said Werner’s approach is built differently.
“Werner approaches military recruitment not as a promotional campaign, but as a core talent pipeline embedded across operations,” Hamm said.
The numbers support that. Approximately 15% of Werner’s workforce are veterans, military spouses or currently serving. The company also keeps a dedicated military recruiting team made up entirely of veterans, people who understand the nuances of military-to-civilian transitions because they have made that transition themselves.
Team driving sits inside that strategy by design. “Team driving serves as a natural bridge within that strategy,” Hamm said. The logic comes from how service members already work. “Service members are accustomed to operational partnerships, shared accountability and working under tight schedules,” he said.
Werner recruits veteran team pairings in several forms: two veterans who served together, a veteran paired with a spouse or relative or solo drivers matched through Werner’s internal Team Matching program. The carrier gives those teams priority on the freight where uptime matters most. “Teams receive high priority on dedicated, expedited and drop-and-hook routes, providing veterans with higher equipment turnaround, strong earning potential and the camaraderie inherent to military units,” Hamm said.
Why the skills transfer
When you ask fleet executives what makes a great driver and the answer usually involve judgment, discipline and comfort with equipment. Hamm said veterans tend to arrive with all three.
“Veterans possess foundational traits that align seamlessly with commercial motor vehicle (CMV) driving,” he said, and he pointed to three in particular.
Safety First . Hamm explained that “the military instills risk assessment protocols and strict adherence to standard operating procedures (SOPs).” In trucking, he said, that matters because managing blind spots, traffic, tight spaces and pre- and post-trip inspections is paramount, so the habit “directly translates to reduced incident rates.”
Heavy equipment is nothing new. “Many military occupational specialties (MOS) involve operating or maintaining heavy tactical vehicles, tracked equipment or complex logistics networks, removing the intimidation factor of operating an 80,000-lb tractor-trailer,” Hamm said.
Remain cool under pressure . For anyone who has run freight through a January storm or a rerouted delivery window, the comparison is easy to draw. “Military personnel are trained to handle uncertain plans, severe weather and dynamic environments without compromising mission objectives,” Hamm said.
Programs that reduce friction
Recruiting veterans takes more than a welcoming message. The transition has a cost, and carriers that ignore it lose candidates to the first employer that doesn’t. Hamm described Werner’s programs as “structured, federally certified pathways designed to minimize friction and maximize earning power during the civilian transition.”
The apprenticeship program is what makes this transition seamless. “Werner launched the industry’s first Registered Truck Driver Apprenticeship,” Hamm said. The program is approved by the Department of Labor and the VA. Eligible veterans can use GI Bill® or VA educational benefits to receive a tax-free monthly housing allowance directly from the VA, on top of their full Werner paycheck, while they complete on-the-job training. “An eligible veteran can earn up to $37,020 tax-free over the course of two years,” Hamm said.
For service members who have already operated heavy equipment in uniform, there are two other routes. Those who did so within two years of leaving military service, can have their platoon commander sign the Military Skills Test Waiver and submit it to their DMV, which waives the road test. The Even Exchange Program waives the knowledge test in participating states. Werner then recognizes that experience once the driver is hired. “For drivers who obtain their CDL through either program, Werner credits your military experience upon hire, qualifying you for a higher pay rate and a wider variety of account options,” Hamm said.
Education support extends beyond the cab. Werner offers CDL school tuition reimbursement of up to $15,000, including GI Bill® tuition reimbursement. It also offers education assistance through discounts with various university’s providing up to $2,500 per year.
Recognition and community are part of the package as well. The Operation Freedom Fleet is Werner’s flagship military recognition fleet, featuring custom-wrapped, military-tribute Kenworth, Peterbilt and Freightliner tractors. The trucks are awarded to currently serving or veteran drivers who maintain spotless safety and service records. Selection to drive one honors the driver’s service and includes attendance at military installations, industry expos, corporate events and school outreach events. Internally, the WEVets associate resource group connects military drivers, shop technicians, office associates and military spouses nationwide for mentorship, transition support, community engagement and career development.
Reframing team driving
Team driving is often the harder sell, even to experienced drivers. Hamm said the best way to address that is to walk through what teams get and then take on the common objections.
On earnings, the structure is different from solo driving. “Werner attributes pay directly to the truck rather than just individual wheel time,” Hamm said. Because team trucks can legally run 4,500 to 5,500+ miles per week by rotating duty cycles, both drivers benefit from split mileage rates that consistently outpace solo weekly miles.
Freight and equipment are the second draw. Team units handle expedited, high-priority and coast-to-coast dedicated freight, and Hamm said Werner prioritizes teams for the newest tractors in its fleet, typically under 1.5 to 2 years old, along with predominantly drop-and-hook customer accounts.
Safety is the third. “Having a co-driver provides a built-in spotter during tight backing maneuvers, a secondary navigator in complex urban corridors and companionship that helps combat highway fatigue,” Hamm said.
Hamm also addressed three misconceptions he hears often.
Teams never get any rest while the truck is rolling. Hamm said modern tractors have changed that. They are engineered with advanced cab suspension systems, custom premium sleeper mattresses and noise-dampening insulation to ensure the off-duty driver gets restorative rest.
A driver must already have a partner . Many teams are husband-and-wife or military buddies, but that isn’t a requirement. “Werner’s structured Team Matching program pairs drivers based on personality, smoking preferences, route interests and geographic home-time hubs,” Hamm said.
Team drivers give up all personal space . Hamm said the reality is more orderly. “Team drivers establish clear shift boundaries, communication norms, and route splits, creating an efficient and predictable work rhythm,” he said. For veterans used to defined roles and clear communication, that structure should feel familiar.
What onboarding looks like
A driver’s first few weeks usually decide whether they stay. Hamm said Werner’s process “accommodates varying levels of prior experience,” and it starts the same way for everyone. Orientation runs two to three days at a Werner terminal. Drivers complete DOT physical screenings, road evaluations, regulatory compliance briefings and instruction on Werner’s proprietary cab technology systems and workflow apps.
After orientation, the path depends on background. Drivers who hold a CDL through the Military Skills Test Waiver go through an accelerated finishing phase. It focuses on civilian DOT compliance, electronic logging devices (ELDs), sliding tandems and customer service, not basic vehicle handling. New entrants and CDL school graduates complete a multi-week on-road mentorship under a certified Werner Driver Leader. They earn a set weekly salary while they work on freight handling, winter driving, trip planning, customer communication and backing maneuvers.
Veterans in the Registered Apprenticeship program get extra administrative support. The military recruiting team coordinates the submission of all Werner and VA paperwork, as well as monthly certifications directly to the VA, so drivers don’t have to manage the process themselves. Once mentoring is complete, drivers or teams are assigned their permanent truck and route network, whether Dedicated, 48-state OTR or Regional.
Support beyond the paycheck
Retention depends on what a driver’s life looks like away from the highway, and for veterans with families, that matters a great deal. Hamm said Werner’s operating model includes infrastructure aimed at those needs.
Concerning scheduling, dedicated fleets, used in specific retail accounts, closed-loop manufacturing and expedited parcel freight, offer “predictable routing, pre-scheduled home time and stable weekly pay guarantees,” Hamm said.
Family support is part of the structure too. “Werner extends Career Currency to family members of drivers and mechanics,” he said.
Health coverage includes comprehensive medical, dental and vision after 30 days of active employment, a company-matched 401(k), and on-site medical clinics at major terminal facilities. Werner also offers pet and authorized passenger ride-along programs. “To support mental well-being and flexibility, Werner offers both pet and authorized passenger ride-along programs,” Hamm said. For teams, and for any driver who spends weeks away from home, those policies can make a real difference.
Where this leaves carriers
Werner’s approach points to a broader lesson for fleets weighing how to recruit veterans. The strongest programs treat military experience as a skill set with real operational value, give it credit in pay and account placement, and pair it with a structure that mirrors how service members already work. Team driving, in Hamm’s framing, is one of the places where all of that comes together.
Veterans bring discipline, equipment familiarity and a habit of working as part of a unit. A carrier that builds pathways for those strengths, from apprenticeship to team matching to a dedicated recruiting staff made up of fellow veterans, gives itself a better chance of turning a first job in trucking into a long career.

Tesla is rolling out stricter driver monitoring for its “Full Self-Driving” system in Europe, with earlier warnings, a full strike for drivers who look away during a manoeuvre, and a hands-on-wheel requirement above 130 km/h (81 mph).
In the US, Tesla has spent the last year going the other way. Its CEO told owners they can text and drive on FSD, and recent US builds were tuned to nag drivers less.
What changes in Europe
On November 16, the Dutch vehicle authority RDW announced that it signed off on a new update to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for FSD (Supervised) in Europe. It covers HW4 vehicles and goes out over the air.
According to the RDW, drivers now get attention warnings earlier. If a driver isn’t paying attention while the system performs a manoeuvre, they get a “full strike.” The regulator says the update also adds measures to prevent misuse of the system, but it didn’t spell out what they are.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
There’s a speed component too. Above 130 km/h (where legal), the driver has to keep their hands on the wheel. And setting a maximum speed above what the system displays now requires the driver to confirm it by scrolling the wheel up, with the speed limit sign pulsing red when the car goes over.
The RDW says it tested the update on its own track and on public roads and found no adverse or unintended effects. Ten other countries have adopted the Dutch approval so far, with Finland now on the list, while EU-wide approval is still waiting on a vote at the TCMV, the committee of member states.
This comes two weeks after Tesla cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe and dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name there. Germany had made both a condition of supporting EU approval.
Meanwhile, in the US
Now look at how Tesla handles the same software at home.
At Tesla’s shareholder meeting last November, Musk complained that the car was “a little strict about keeping your eyes on the road” and said Tesla would “allow you to text and drive essentially” within a month or two. A month later, an owner asked whether FSD v14.2.1 allowed texting. Musk’s answer : “Depending on context of surrounding traffic, yes.”
Texting while driving is illegal in 49 states. FSD is still a Level 2 system, and Tesla’s own fine print says the driver is responsible at all times.
In May, Musk confirmed that FSD v14.3.3 was built to nag drivers less. Tesla did add better eye-gaze tracking and eyewear handling in a June build, to be fair. But the pitch to owners hasn’t changed: fewer nags is sold as a feature.
And US drivers have been allowed to go hands-free on FSD at any speed since Tesla moved to cabin-camera monitoring in 2024. There’s no 130 km/h rule here.
NHTSA noticed. In its engineering analysis of FSD crashes in low-visibility conditions, the agency asked Tesla to justify a list of its marketing claims, and it specifically cited Musk’s texting post. In September, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi asked NHTSA to look into Tesla’s driver monitoring after dozens of videos appeared to show drivers asleep on Autopilot and FSD.
The results are on the road. Last month, a driver told the CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove through a freeway closure and hit a patrol car, seriously injuring two officers. Owners are also filming themselves defeating Tesla’s driver monitoring and posting it for clout.
Same car, two standards
Both markets get the same cabin camera and the same HW4 computer.
But in Europe, a type-approval authority tests every update before it ships and can refuse it. In the US, nobody pre-approves driver-assist software. Tesla self-certifies, and NHTSA only steps in after complaints and crashes pile up, which is how you end up with a CEO publicly telling owners to text while the regulator is still writing letters about it.
Electrek’s Take
This update proves Tesla can build stricter driver monitoring whenever a regulator demands it. The code exists. It’s running on HW4 cars in 11 European countries right now.
That makes the US approach hard to defend. Tesla’s argument for relaxing supervision is that FSD is now good enough. But if that were true, it would be showing the RDW data proving looser monitoring is safe, not adding earlier warnings and harsher strikes to get approved. It’s doing the opposite in Europe because it has to, and the opposite of that in the US because it can.
We’ve been saying it for a while: FSD gets more dangerous as it gets better , because people trust it more and watch the road less. The answer is monitoring that tightens as the system improves. Europe is forcing exactly that. In the US, Tesla is loosening it, encouraging illegal phone use from the top, and leaving drivers with 100% of the liability when it goes wrong.
So here’s the question for Tesla. If European owners are getting earlier warnings and instant strikes, why not American owners on the exact same software? Or is NHTSA going to have to force it?

U.S. last-mile delivery prices rose 10.5% year over year in the third quarter, three times the 3.5% increase in consumer prices, according to a new quarterly index that logistics provider GEODIS launched this week.
What’s Related
The U.S. Final Mile Index tracks prices for two types of delivery that shippers often budget for separately. It covers parcel deliveries to households and local freight deliveries to businesses . The first edition also covers diesel prices, driver conditions, cargo theft and delivery performance.
How it works
GEODIS uses two U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price indexes, one for couriers and messengers and the other for local general freight trucking . It sets both series to 100 in 2019 and gives them equal weight. Together, they reached 149.8 in the third quarter, putting delivery prices 49.8% above the 2019 baseline. Consumer prices rose 30.8% over the same stretch, according to GEODIS.
The index gives shippers a benchmark for reviewing carrier rate increases or building a transportation budget. Because the headline number gives parcel and local trucking prices equal weight, a shipper that sends mostly packages may get a more relevant comparison from the parcel figures. A business that relies on local freight deliveries can look at the trucking figures separately.
RELATED: Delivery Reliability Now Matters as Much as Speed, Survey Finds
Fuel and missed deliveries add to the bill
The report puts the third-quarter price increase alongside a spike in diesel. The national average for on-highway diesel reached a record $6.53 a gallon in the week of Sept. 21, about 74% above its level a year earlier. Fuel surcharges can add to what shippers pay even when their base rates stay the same.
GEODIS also looks at what happens when a shipment arrives late or short. It points to Walmart , which charges suppliers 3% of the cost of goods on cases that miss its on-time or in-full requirements. In GEODIS’s example, a supplier shipping $100 million in goods annually would face $300,000 in penalties if late or short cases accounted for 10% of that value. Redelivery or expedited shipping can add to the bill.
Theft losses on the rise
The report flags warehouses and distribution centers as a point of exposure before the final delivery leg. GEODIS says those sites accounted for 37% of second-quarter cargo theft incidents.
In the U.S. and Canada , Verisk CargoNet recorded 677 supply chain theft incidents in the second quarter, down 26% from a year earlier. Estimated losses more than doubled to $304.6 million, driven in part by several multimillion-dollar thefts. CargoNet’s figures cover supply chain theft across transportation modes.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 18, 2026
Rua Gold’s (TSX: RUA; NZX: RGI) proposed Auld Creek gold-antimony project in New Zealand has lost its economic case as a standalone operation after tests showed the plant would recover little more than half the antimony in its feed. The stock dropped. A prefeasibility study (PFS) released late Tuesday puts Auld Creek’s after-tax net present value (NPV) at negative $30.5 million (negative C$43.6 million), discounted at 5%. May’s preliminary economic assessment put it at positive $42.4 million. Expected antimony recovery fell to 54% from 85%, the main reason for the reversal, even as the assumed gold price rose to $3,700 per oz. from $3,300, Rua said.
“We view the Auld Creek PFS as negative, with lower antimony recovery driving a negative NPV, though it does allow permitting to progress under the fast track Approvals process,” ATB Cormark Capital Markets mining analyst Richard Gray said Wednesday in a note. “A viable project now rests on metallurgical work to lift antimony recovery and on adding Globe Progress through a hub-and-spoke plan.” Rua shares sank 9% to 99¢ Wednesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$114 million ($80 million). The stock has ranged from 98¢ to C$2 in the past year. ATB Cormark’s Gray cut his target price on Rua to C$1.45 from C$2 following the study’s release. He kept his “speculative buy” rating on the stock.
Engineering foundation
To justify building a plant on New Zealand’s South Island, Rua is testing whether it can recover more antimony and whether the nearby Globe Progress deposit could supply additional feed. Rua has declared no mineral reserve.
“The Auld Creek study provides a detailed engineering foundation and identifies the work needed to establish a viable development case,” CEO Robert Eckford said in the release. The study estimates $133.5 million of pre-production capital for an underground operation and a plant treating 250,000 tonnes a year. Over 5.6 years, Rua would recover about 78,800 oz. of gold and 4,350 tonnes of antimony. The assumed gold recovery held at 95%, while the assumed antimony price eased to $26,000 a tonne from $27,000 in May’s assessment. Globe Progress, where open-pit mining ended in 2016, has indicated resources of 190,000 tonnes at 2.28 g/t gold for 14,000 oz. and inferred resources of 4.4 million tonnes at 2.44 g/t gold for 346,000 oz., as of Nov. 3. Rua still has to test how the Globe Progress material would respond to processing.

Parked and Forgotten: 1969 Daimler Sovereign Is Wasting Away in Very Old Barn

Photo: IMSTOKZE/YouTube
When it comes to barn-found classics, I love the stories in which the vehicles get rescued and revived . Sadly, these stories aren't very common. Most barn finds never get a second chance and end up wasting away. This old British sedan is one of those rigs.
We're looking at a Daimler Sovereign, which is an iconic part of British automotive history. Although it may not be particularly famous outside the UK, Daimler is a big name on the island, particularly for having supplied cars to the royal family from 1902 until the 1950s.
Purchased by the Birmingham Small Arms Company in 1910, Daimler became a part of Jaguar in 1960. The latter began using the name on upscale versions of its cars. In 1968, Daimler got a standalone model called the DS420, which became an official state car in many countries.
This Daimler is a Sovereign, which debuted in 1966 as a more luxurious version of the Jaguar 420 sedan, which in turn was based on the S-Type. In 1969, the Sovereign name was transferred to the brand-new XJ6 architecture. The car you see here is a first-year model, and, according to the owner, it's also one of the first examples ever made.
Unfortunately, this Daimler spent a lot of time in a very old barn. The owner reportedly bought it for restoration. The car was still running and driving at the time it was parked. But as is often the case, life got in the way, and the owner never got around to start the restoration.
It's unclear when it was parked, but it must have been sitting for decades. The blue paint is heavily weathered, while the interior sustained notable damage due to prolonged exposure to moisture. The original engine is still under the hood, but it looks like it will need a rebuild to fire up again.
By the way, the XJ6 it is based on was offered with Jaguar's iconic XK inline-six engine. Owners could choose between the 2.8 or 4.2-liter version. The former came with 104 horsepower on tap, while the latter delivered 246 horsepower. The XJ6 and Sovereign were the last Jaguars powered by the XK engine.
The owner says he is now too old to take care of the car, and it's unclear whether he wants to sell it or not. Whatever the case, this Daimler needs a new home ASAP because it's pretty close to the point where it's no longer worth restoring.
These cars aren't particularly valuable, though. They rarely fetch over $30,000 at public auctions, with most examples having sold for well under $20,000 in recent years. All told, the restoration would have to be a labor of love . Hit the play button below to check it out. The Dailmer footage starts at the 16-minute mark.

With so many custom garages taking care of Americans' appetite for modified vehicles, you'd think the market is saturated, and there's little room for newcomers to come in and play the game. Think again, as the Hennessey Group thinks quite the opposite.
Out of the blue, the behemoth that also happens to own Hennessey Performance , the makers of the $2.5 Blackbird, among other things, announced the launch of something called the 1776 Off-Road. That would be the makers of upgrades of all shapes and sizes for the likes of the Ram 1500 and Ram 2500 pickup trucks.
To make sure everybody notices the newcomer's arrival on the national market, the Texas-based crew also released the initial details of some specially prepped pickup trucks from the above-mentioned families, and let me tell you, they are quite something to behold.
The trucks were born after they've been fitted with 1776's first two customization packages. And I'll start with the smaller of the two, which is at the same time my favorite one of the pair.
Photo: 1776 The 1776 Off-Road comes along with whatever powertrain customers choose off the factory floor, and many of the stock components as well, but adds on top of everything a lot of extras to make it meaner and more capable.
The customizer included in the package, first and foremost, new hardware for translating more effectively the engine's power into forward or backward motion, regardless of the terrain it travels over. We've got, thus, 22-inch off-road wheels fitted with 35-inch all-terrain tires and tied to a completely new off-road suspension system. There's also a lift at play, with six inches of extra ground clearance gained this way on both ends.
For the truck's powertrain, 1776 provides a stainless cat-back exhaust system with black tips. For easier access, the sides of the 1500 are now fitted with power running boards. Visual enhancements include painted off-road fender flares, while the front displays a grille-mounted LED light bar. The bedside is decorated as well, in this case with a special Stars & Stripes vinyl livery.
The interior was not left to chance either, with WeatherTech front and rear floor liners matching diamond-quilted leather and Alcantara seats and an interior console plaque being installed.
Photo: 1776 The bigger Ram 2500 can be upgraded over at 1776 as well, and it too becomes even meaner by throwing into the battle even more aftermarket hardware. It all starts, just like in the case of the 1500, underneath the bodywork.
This truck rides on a BDS four-inch suspension system at the front and BDS 2.5-inch coil springs at the rear. The setup includes high-clearance tubular radius arms, performance shock absorbers, and a dual steering stabilizer, and it too is connected to 22-inch off-road wheels on all corners, this time shod in larger, 37-inch all-terrain tires. The custom crew opted to include a performance exhaust tip in the package.
From here onward, there are a lot of similarities with the solutions offered for the 1500: color-matched fender flares, LED off-road light pods mounted on the A-pillar, WeatherTech front and rear floor liners inside, diamond-quilted leather and Alcantara seats, and an interior console-mounted plaque, among others. Why, there are even the same raised exterior badges.
1776 says it offers both packages complete with a three-year, 36,000-mile (58,000 km) bumper-to-bumper warranty, but makes no mention of how much each of the packages is worth in this exact form. Not even the company's website, already up and running, is more revealing in that respect.
Photo: 1776 No matter how much 1776 will charge for these upgrades, it's important to note that every single sale will be matched with a donation of undisclosed size made to the Folds of Honor, a charity that provides educational scholarships to wives and kids of fallen or disabled soldiers and first responders.
The two packages designed for the two Ram trucks are, according to 1776, only the beginning, as more will follow in the not-so-distant future, and they'll cover pickups made by other companies as well, Ford and GM. I'll keep an eye on that, as I can't wait to see what their trucks will look like with such things on.
As for where you'll find these upgrades, the company website I mentioned earlier is not the only way to go. The 1776 packages and upgrades will be sold through participating Ram dealers, but you’ll have to check if your local one made the cut.
Hennessey hopes the newly-founded customization company will live and and thrive in this segment, and it's probably not wrong. Americans not only buy pickup trucks like there's no tomorrow, but a large chunk of them also decide what the factory offers is not enough, so they turn to customizers the likes of 1776. As for the choice of name made for this new crew, I think it needs little introduction, especially this year.

The Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator is helping the postage stamp nation of Luxembourg connect natural freshwater springs to a planned water reservoir, but the work has to be done in an existing groundwater protection zone, where even the smallest fuel spills or oil leaks could have serious consequences. An ideal opportunity, in other words, for a battery electric machine like the EWR150 Electric to shine .
“Sometimes I miss the sound of the engine,” says Thomas Weber, an operator on the project who’d previously worked with the conventional EWR150 wheeled excavator. “But the quieter operation of the EWR150 Electric is more beneficial for me, personally. Compared to the diesel equivalent, I find the performance and power to be identical.”
Volvo CE took to LinkedIn to share the work being done by the Luxemburgers at construction firm Elenz, touting the Volvo’s clean, quiet running in this highly environment.
