Intel is doing a mini launch of its next-generation server CPU (or something thereabouts at SC26). There are many systems on the floor, but one, the Bull Sequana XH31600, actually showed Diamond Rapids packages.
Bull Shows Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids Package at SC26
Starting off, here is the Bull compute blade with blind mate power and liquid at the rear, networking in front, and four Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids packages up front.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 2
Just ot be clear about what you are seeing, these are two dual-socket compute nodes with Intel Diamond Rapids, each with 16-channel memory.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 1
Here is a view of the package. We have already seen the LGA9324 socket covered in the ASRock Rack DMRD16-2L+ from OCP Summit 2026.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 Intel Diamond Rapids Package 4
You can see that in the Bull platform, the CPUs are on fairly wide motherboards because of all of the memory on either side.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 9
The idea is that these blades are liquid cooled, so you can see how everything has heatpipes and liquid cooling blocks.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 2
The other node had the liquid cooling blocks as well as the cabled connections to the networking.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 5
On the networking, Bull had its BXI technology for interconnect. In its booth, Bull showed a BXI switch with 64x 800G OSFP ports, but the BXI NICs were shown as QSFP-DD and PCIe Gen5 x16. It actually looks like Bull is doing something similar to what we did with the NVIDIA ConnectX-8 C8240 800G Dual 400G NIC Review This is a SuperNIC when we managed to use two PCIe Gen5 x16 links to get 800Gbps from the ConnectX-8.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 12
What stood out a bit is that there was an NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC as well in an OCP NIC 3.0 form factor. It’s interesting that Bull has its own interconnect, with a 51.2T switch and a PCIe Gen5 NIC in a platform with a Gen6 CPU, but right next to it is NVIDIA’s high-volume PCIe Gen6 NIC competitor.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 13
What is very cool about this platform is that it is incredibly bespoke.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 14
For years, Bull has had one of the better-looking blade designs, largely because they liquid-cool everything. Probably worth pondering, however, is that with NVIDIA pushing the industry with ORv3, and AMD now with the double-wide. It feels like there is a high-volume standard for high-density racks in the industry if you want power and cooling. Maybe the more interesting part is that Bull’s design does not have a copper-cabled backplane in the rear.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 15
Overall, this was very neat to see.
Final Words
What has been interesting at SC26 is that this type of platform would have been mind-blowing years ago. Now, with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin designs in ORv3 racks, the Bull systems fit in with the higher-volume AI infrastructure bits. What Bull has, however, is SiPearl, Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids, NVIDIA, and AMD Venice nodes on display in a common form factor.
Bull SC26 Chicago-Bull Sequana XH31600 Intel Diamond Rapids Package 1
Many other vendors are showing off Diamond Rapids systems with neat designs, including 32DIMM/ socket 2DPC configurations at SC26. For its part, Bull is the only one we have found that has a package. Diamond Rapids seems to be in the sampling phase. The best guess is maybe we start to see a launch in Q2 2027, but if that slips past June (or it becomes a split launch with 1P platforms and 2P platforms), the next real launch window for Intel is early September 2027.

Tesla has opened its first Semi Megacharger in Texas, an 8-stall station in Mesquite on the east side of Dallas. With it, Tesla’s map now lists 7 public Megacharger sites and 44 stalls for its electric truck.
That’s progress. But with six weeks left in 2026, it’s less than a fifth of the 37 sites Tesla planned to have open this year.
Texas finally gets one
Tesla Charging announced the new station on X on Tuesday night with its usual one-liner and a photo of the stalls at sunset:
New Tesla Megacharger: Mesquite, TX (8 stalls) https://t.co/UsCFMyCjo7 pic.twitter.com/W4G1e2BHkb — Tesla Charging (@TeslaCharging) November 18, 2026
Tesla’s map lists the site at 2175 S Town East Blvd in Mesquite, with eight Megachargers rated at up to 1.2 MW each.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Texas is where Tesla has the most riding on this network. When Tesla added 64 Megacharger locations to its map in February , Texas got 19 of the 66 planned sites, more than any other state. Mesquite is the first of them to go live, and several other Dallas–Fort Worth sites are still marked “coming soon.”
The Pilot truck stop rollout hasn’t reached Texas either. When Pilot opened its first Megacharger in Georgia in October, it named a Flying J in Fort Stockton, Texas, as one of the next sites. It’s still not live on Tesla’s map.
Tesla also isn’t alone in DFW. Greenlane, the truck charging joint venture between Daimler Truck, NextEra and BlackRock, announced high-power sites in Dallas and Houston in May, open to any electric truck with CCS and MCS connectors. Tesla now has a station operating in the metro.
The whole network fits in a short list
Here’s every public Megacharger currently live on Tesla’s map:
Bloomington, CA: 6 stalls
Vernon, CA: 6 stalls
Tulare, CA (Pilot/Flying J): 4 stalls
Conley, GA (south of Atlanta): 8 stalls
Ellabell, GA (Pilot, west of Savannah): 6 stalls
Hodgkins, IL (southwest of Chicago): 6 stalls
Mesquite, TX: 8 stalls
That’s 7 sites and 44 stalls in four states. When we counted in early October , there were four customer-facing sites with 26 stalls. Tulare opened the same week, Hodgkins came on November 10, and now Mesquite.
So Tesla is adding a site roughly every two weeks.
Tesla also runs private Megachargers for its own fleet at Giga Nevada and in Carson, California, and it sells Megachargers to fleets and depot operators through its business program. Forum Mobility switched on two at the Port of Long Beach earlier this month. None of those count toward the public network that Semi buyers without their own depot rely on.
The 37-site math doesn’t work
Tesla’s Q4 2025 shareholder report showed about 37 Megacharger sites for 2026. Semi program lead Dan Priestley has said Tesla wants 46 by early 2027.

To me this seems like good progress, sure it's not right on time with their ambitious goal, but they are executing on their charging network and I'm sure more sites will keep opening.

To hit 37, Tesla would need to open 30 more sites in the next 43 days. At the current pace, it ends the year with around 10.
Pilot said in October that nine more of its sites were under construction, so a late burst is possible. But it would have to be a very big one.
And the trucks are starting to show up. Tesla launched volume production of the Semi in September at a Nevada factory it says can build 50,000 trucks a year, and it said last week that Chicago’s first 50 Semis are en route for delivery, a day after Hodgkins opened. Big fleets like that customer are installing their own depot chargers anyway, and most Semi charging will happen there. The public network is what lets a Semi leave its home region.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 18, 2026
Platinum could swing from a 468,000-oz. surplus this year to a 279,000-oz. deficit in 2027 as investors buy more bars and coins, exchange inventories rebuild and mine supply slips, the World Platinum Investment Council said Wednesday in its first forecast for next year. The council expects investment demand to swing by 911,000 oz., more than the entire 747,000-oz. change in the market balance. It projects net investment of 513,000 oz. next year after outflows this year. Bar and coin purchases would climb 55% to 448,000 oz. and exchange warehouses would add 110,000 oz. Investors would still withdraw 150,000 oz. from exchange-traded funds, according to the quarterly outlook prepared for the council by Metals Focus. “Platinum above ground stocks remain critically depleted with the forecast surplus in 2026 following three consecutive years of significant deficit,” council CEO Trevor Raymond said in a release.
Limited inventory
The forecast leaves little inventory to absorb a supply disruption if buying resumes. Above-ground stocks would fall to 1.81 million oz. by the end of next year, enough to cover just under three months of global demand. This year’s surplus, enlarged by 203,000 oz. from the previous forecast, would leave about three and a half months’ cover at year-end. Industrial users offer the other source of growth. Use is forecast to rise 4% to a record 2.66 million oz. as gains in chemicals and petroleum outweigh declines in glass and electrical applications. Automakers are expected to use 5% less platinum, or 2.81 million oz., as battery-electric vehicles gain ground and some manufacturers switch back to palladium in catalytic converters. Mine supply could fall 1% to 5.57 million oz., with growth in Zimbabwe offsetting only part of South Africa’s decline. Metals Focus expects recycling to rise 5% to 1.85 million oz., enough to lift total supply by 1%. Demand would rise 12%.

Sedona Is a Gorgeous A-Frame Park Model With Big Windows, Warm Wood, and Cabin Charm

Photo: Amberwood Tiny Homes
It’s true that tiny living often trades everyday comfort and luxury for minimalism and simplicity. However, many modern tiny homes are no longer about cramped spaces and basic amenities. On the contrary, models like the Sedona show that tiny homes can feel surprisingly opulent if designed with eye-catching silhouettes, smart layouts, and high-end finishes.
The thought of moving into a tiny home doesn’t have to make you anxious and concerned about cramped interiors and a lack of comfort. A well-designed compact dwelling will turn tight square footage into a calm, functional space, making you feel at ease rather than boxed in.
This is entirely true for the Sedona tiny home, which combines 432 square feet (40.1 square meters) of residential-style living space with a beautiful A-frame design and a structure built for year-round living. In addition, this model comes with inviting living zones, complete amenities, and cozy, cabin-style aesthetics.
The Sedona is the creation of Amberwood Tiny Homes, a Canadian manufacturer based in Bow Island, Alberta, that is part of the Hiebert Group and delivers across North America. The company offers various types of compact dwellings, including foundation tiny homes, tiny homes on wheels, and park model homes, all built to the highest standards with four-season living, durability, and flexibility in mind.
Photo: Amberwood Tiny Homes Measuring 36 feet (10.9 meters) long and 12 feet (3.6 meters) wide, the Sedona qualifies as a park model RV , which means it offers a more generous layout, better amenities, and more style than standard towable tiny houses. The only caveat is that, due to its oversized dimensions, it’s not meant to be towed frequently. It’s a unit designed for more permanent living arrangements, suitable for private properties, vacation retreats, and resort communities.
Far from a traditional tiny home on wheels , this park model catches the eye with a rectangular structure and a pitched roof at the front and an A-frame-inspired section at the rear. The combination gives it a contemporary architectural silhouette while still preserving some of the visual appeal of a traditional cabin.
The exterior is clad in a mix of black corrugated metal and natural wood accents, complemented by a durable metal roof and black-framed windows that further enhance its modern appearance. A huge A-frame window at the rear adds another contemporary touch, flooding the interior with natural light and making this model ideal for placement in scenic locations, like a mountain resort, a wooded property, or near a lake.
Photo: Amberwood Tiny Homes Patio glass doors open to reveal a lush, premium interior that offers all the comforts of a brick-and-mortar home. Designed primarily for two occupants, the Sedona boasts a spacious layout in which each living area feels residential without the downsides typically associated with tiny living. There is room for an inviting lounge, a full kitchen, a spacious downstairs bedroom, and a practical bathroom, as well as a storage loft, all within a configuration that flows naturally and separates common areas from the private ones.
Style-wise, the interior combines contemporary finishes with warm, cabin-inspired details. Natural wood covers the walls and ceiling in the living area, creating a mountain cabin ambiance, but just a few feet away, the kitchen is completely modern, with black and white cabinetry, gray marble countertops, and stainless steel appliances.
The most alluring area is definitely the picturesque A-frame living room, with its full wall of black-framed windows that make the outdoors an integral part of the living experience. Cozy and snug, this area of the house is fitted with comfortable seating arrangements, providing a nice place to gather with friends or relax in solitude.
Photo: Amberwood Tiny Homes With a U-shaped design, the kitchen feels like a proper residential cooking space and offers exceptional functionality. It’s equipped with a full suite of appliances, including a full range, a venting hood, a dual-bowl sink, a full-size refrigerator, and a dishwasher, while a multitude of cabinets ensure there is sufficient storage for cooking essentials.
White upper cabinets contrast with the dark countertops and black lower cabinets, while the white tile backsplash adds another contemporary detail. The design also integrates a large peninsula with pendant lights and barstools, providing a nice space for dining. This peninsula also creates a seamless link between the lounge and kitchen, transforming it into a gathering space when friends come over.
The bedroom, situated at the end of a narrow corridor, is bright and charming, with a design that blends modern and rustic elements. A queen-size bed is set against a black accent wall and flanked by two narrow, vertical windows, and a wardrobe is included opposite it for clothes storage. The natural wood-planked ceiling and a barn-style door add rustic coziness to the space.
Photo: Amberwood Tiny Homes The same exquisite sense of style is evident in the bathroom, which combines forest green shiplap walls with a natural wood accent wall, a black vanity, and modern lighting. Though not very large, it includes all the fixtures needed for full-time living , including a washer and dryer. There is also a loft above the bathroom, accessed by a wooden ladder from the hallway. It has a low ceiling and features a window for ventilation, which means it could also be used for sleeping if necessary.
Less visible but equally important for comfortable everyday living, features like in-floor heating, dual-zone air conditioning, and four-season insulation make this tiny home appropriate for four-season use.
Bringing together the practicality of a park model RV and the visual appeal of a contemporary A-frame retreat, the Sedona tiny home makes downsizing feel indulgent. Price-wise, a unit similar to the one pictured here starts at CAD $205,198 (USD $143,166) plus taxes.

Merck is canning multiple Phase 3 studies of nemtabrutinib after a benefit-risk review derailed hopes of the asset entering the non-covalent BTK inhibitor race.
Merck is ending development of an experimental oral BTK inhibitor after identifying safety risks, a move that includes shuttering several late-stage studies.
The asset, known as nemtabrutinib or MK-1026 and picked up in the $2.7 billion buyout of ArQule at the end of 2019, was being evaluated in a series of hematology studies making up Merck’s BELLWAVE program. The New Jersey pharma shared Tuesday evening that the entire program would be discontinued, including three Phase 3 studies.
The decision stems from an external recommendation from a data monitoring committee that reviewed findings from the late-stage BELLWAVE-011 trial for patients with untreated chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL). Merck launched the trial in 2023 and expected to recruit 1,200 patients, with a primary readout slated for 2032.
The data committee suggested that the potential benefits of nemtabrutinib may not outweigh the risks in the study. Merck “subsequently confirmed this following a review of the data in its totality” and also decided to terminate the broader program, the company said in the release.
That includes shuttering the BELLWAVE-008 trial for certain patients with CLL/SLL and BELLWAVE-010 for second-line advanced CLL/SLL.

The non-covalent BTK inhibitor, formerly known as ARQ 531, was the centerpiece of the ArQule deal. At the time, the asset had demonstrated a manageable safety profile and early signs of anti-tumor activity in a Phase 1 study.
The acquisition gave Merck a spot in the BTK inhibitor race after Eli Lilly’s $8 billion buy of Loxo Oncology. In early 2023, Lilly gained accelerated approval in mantle cell lymphoma for the Loxo-discovered Jaypirca—the first FDA-approved non-covalent BTK inhibitor to reach the market. The drug later received expanded approval for CLL/SLL.
Jaypirca’s label warns about the risk of infections, bleeding, low blood cell counts, abnormal heart rhythms, new cancers, liver damage and embryo-fetal toxicity.
Merck’s discontinuation comes as the pharma braces for looming patent expiries for its blockbuster cancer therapy Keytruda. Patent losses starting in 2028 will put $33 billion in revenue at risk, according to a September report from BMO. But analysts have been largely bullish on the company’s plans to replace the key revenue stream, highlighting the Moderna-partnered mRNA cancer vaccine intismeran autogene , Winrevair for a rare form of high blood pressure in the lungs and the TROP2 antibody drug conjugate sac-TMT as its strongest potential growth products.

Photo: Pentastic Motors
Buick entered the golden muscle car era with a refined sledgehammer known as the Gran Sport, a high-performance badge affectionately dubbed the Gentleman's Hot Rod. Debuting for the 1965 model year as an option package on the intermediate Skylark, it became a standalone model shortened to GS in 1968. After migrating to the restyled Century platform in 1973, the original classic rear-wheel-drive muscle moniker retired following the 1975 model year.
For the first five years, General Motors enforced a strict 400-cubic-inch displacement ceiling on intermediate automobiles. In truth, the ban forbade more than one cubic inch per ten pounds of vehicle curb weight, which effectively led to the 400-cube cap (it's also much easier to remember than the volume-to-mass ratio).
When corporate leadership finally lifted that restriction for 1970, Buick unleashed the GS 455, installing its thin-wall-cast 455-cubic-inch big-block V8 into the mid-size A-body chassis. Buyers craving maximum dragstrip authority could tick the Stage 1 option, a factory performance package first offered on the 1969 GS 400 and available on the 455 through 1974.
Unlike flashier Detroit packages built around cartoon decals, the Stage 1 option focused purely on internal breathing and valvetrain hardware. Compared to a standard GS 455, a Stage 1 V8 received special cylinder heads relieved around larger 2.125-inch intake and 1.755-inch exhaust valves, stiffer valve springs, and a high-lift camshaft. Engineers also added a recalibrated ignition distributor, a rich-jetted Rochester Quadrajet 4-barrel carburetor, and a mandatory 3.42:1 Positraction rear axle.
Photo: Pentastic Motors Featuring a 4.3125-inch bore and 3.90-inch stroke, the 455-cubic-inch (7.5-liter) Stage 1 V8 boasted 10.0:1 compression in 1970, producing 360 gross hp at 4,600 rpm and 510 lb-ft of torque at 2,800 rpm (365 PS, 692 Nm). It was the torquiest motor of any car in its class – not just GM, but everyone. In fact, it was second only to the Cadillac 500 V8, the 8.2-litre mastodont that spun under 550 lb-ft of crank twist (746 Nm).
For 1971, lower-octane fuel mandates dropped compression to 8.5:1. The base 1971 GS 455 fell to 315 gross hp and 450 lb-ft (319 PS/610 Nm), whereas the Stage 1 delivered 345 gross hp, or 275 net hp, and 460 lb-ft (350/279 PS, 624 Nm).
Period magazine road tests documented the effect of that compression reduction. In January 1970, Motor Trend clocked an automatic 1970 GS 455 Stage 1 from 0 to 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and through the quarter-mile in 13.38 seconds at 105.50 mph, while the 4-speed ran 13.79 seconds at 104.50 mph. Tested for 1971, the Stage 1 hit 60 mph in 6.5 seconds and ran 14.7 seconds at 92.5 mph. Just like that, the EPA added an extra second on the timeslip of the emblematic Muscle Car’s muscle car.
Photo: Pentastic Motors Across all 11 model years from 1965 through 1975, Buick produced a combined 143,945 mid-size Gran Sport and GS automobiles. During the core 1965 to 1972 Skylark and GS era, assembly plants built 132,665 units, comprising 15,780 cars in 1965, 13,816 in 1966, 19,626 in 1967, a record 26,345 in 1968, 19,257 in 1969, 20,096 in 1970, 9,170 in 1971, and 8,575 in 1972. Century GS models added 11,280 units.
Labor strikes and insurance surcharges cut 1971 GS volume by more than 50% compared to the previous season, to 9,170 cars (8,268 hardtops and 902 convertibles), including 124 GSX hardtops. Base GS 350 production totaled 5,986 hardtops, with 25 3-speeds, 358 4-speeds , and 5,603 automatics, plus 656 convertibles (six 3-speeds, 51 4-speeds, and 599 automatics).
Standard GS 455 output reached 1,481 hardtops, with 103 4-speeds and 1,378 automatics, and 165 convertibles, comprising 18 4-speeds and 147 automatics.
Photo: Pentastic Motors The 1971 GS 455 Stage 1 proved far rarer, totaling just 882 units. Only 801 Stage 1 hardtop coupes rolled off the line, divided into 687 Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 automatics and 114 4-speed manuals, while the 81 Stage 1 convertibles included 72 automatics and nine 4-speeds. Priced from $3,449 when new before the $200 Stage 1 option, a 1971 Gran Sport is nowhere near the stratospheric values of other contemporary muscle cars of its day.
Among those 114 factory 4-speed hardtops , one surviving example is on the lookout for a new caretaker. Located in Gorrie, Ontario (Canada, folks), this numbers-matching 1971 Buick GS 455 Stage 1 left the Flint, Michigan assembly plant in January 1971 and sold new at H.J. Foster Motors in Agincourt, Ontario, as 1 of just 337 examples delivered across the Great White North that model year.
Accompanied by General Motors Historical Services paperwork and showing 60,297 miles, the coupe underwent a comprehensive frame-off restoration into its original Code 13 Platinum Mist Poly metallic silver finish. The photographs and the walkaround video (embedded below) confirms razor-sharp panel alignment, mirror-bright chrome, a tight black vinyl roof, red-inlaid Stage 1 fender and decklid emblems, red-striped rocker moldings, and 5-spoke Rallye wheels shod in BFGoodrich Radial T/A tires.
Photo: Pentastic Motors Opening the doors reveals a vintage Sunoco lubrication sticker logged at 59,038 miles. Inside, the restored black vinyl cabin pairs perforated Strato bucket seats and a pristine headliner with rare factory options including power windows, tinted glass, and a tilt steering column.
Under the twin-scooped hood, the numbers-matching 455-cubic-inch V8 wears bright Buick red paint, chrome valve covers, and the dual-snorkel Stage 1 air cleaner with foam seals. Rebuilt to a 9.5:1 compression ratio with a TA Performance camshaft and lifter kit, the big-block mates to a refreshed Muncie M21 4-speed manual with a LuK clutch, spinning a rebuilt 10-bolt Positraction axle with 3.42:1 gears above new Dynomax dual exhaust mufflers.
The undercarriage displays fresh body mount bushings, stainless steel fuel and brake lines, rebuilt steering and suspension, power steering, and power front disc brakes. Currently offered for sale by Pentastic Motors in Gorrie, Ontario, this certified 1971 Buick GS 455 Stage 1 includes a 3-year or 70,000-kilometer (43,500 miles) powertrain warranty and an insurance appraisal for $109,971 CAD plus taxes and licensing, which converts to $76,892 USD at current currency exchange rates. Stranded Woman Turns the 2026 FAA Nationwide Ground Stop Into a 1,600-Mile Ford Bronco Road Trip
6 photos
Photo: @drtaraharding on Instagram
Tara Harding did not fly to Charlotte, North Carolina, with the intention of buying a Ford Bronco. She had a work trip to finish and a flight home to catch. As fate would have it, the FAA had other plans for her, grounding flights nationwide. Her airline repeatedly changed the departure arrangements, and alternatives began disappearing fast.
By the time Tara and two women from her team had exhausted their options, buying a body-on-frame SUV and driving 1,593 miles (2,564 kilometers) back to North Dakota sounded perfectly reasonable to her. This explains how a dealership visit turned into an unexpected nine-state road trip, followed by a surprising decision to keep the Sasquatch Package-equipped Outer Banks.
Harding explained the adventure on her Instagram, describing how the return flights had been rescheduled five times before the final cancellation. With the Federal Aviation Administration grounding flights due to a conflict between new telecom equipment and legacy air traffic control systems, getting out of North Carolina became way harder than simply finding another departure.
Tara and company spent plenty of time looking for alternatives, beginning with rental cars. The problem? None were available within a 4-hour radius. Trains and buses offered no workable solution either. The women also considered renting a U-Haul, but at that point, Harding's mother-in-law proposed buying a vehicle outright. Ka-ching! Surprisingly, Tara took the suggestion seriously.
She and her companions headed to Mark Ficken Ford (and Lincoln), a Charlotte dealer with a 4.6-star rating on Google Maps. Tara purchased the Bronco of her liking with help from salesman Jackson Weaver, whom she thanked publicly on Instagram.
A rather amusing sale, most definitely, especially when you remember that many Bronco customers spend a lot of time comparing trim levels, browsing accessories, and thinking whether a given option is worth the extra dollars.
Photo: @drtaraharding on Instagram The immediate priority was needing some wheels, and for some reason, I just remembered that scene from The Blues Brothers where Elwood says that it's 106 miles to Chicago, they got a full tank of gas, and half a pack of cigs in their 1974 Dodge Monaco. In my imagination, given the circumstances, Tara summoned her inner Jake when deciding to put money down on this nicely spec'd Bronco.
She had considered selling the off-road model after reaching North Dakota, with Tara even joking about putting the Bronco up for sale. She later admitted that a soft spot for it was developing, and who could blame her after so many miles of driving? After all, extraordinary circumstances brought them together.
Harding said the trip was filled with laughter and caffeine. The Ford Motor Company responded to one of Harding's posts, pointing out that such a trip is a great way to get to know her new ride. Speaking of which, the break-in period of a brand-new Bronco is 1,000 miles (a little over 1,600 kilometers).
Tara spent 12 hours in bed after the journey, and her husband also grew a soft spot for the Bronco. Before she even woke up, he had already taken the off-roader out for three drives. That changed the fate of the Bronco, with Tara confirming that her family will be keeping the Desert Sand-painted SUV . The UK's 2027 Jaecoo 7 Luxury+ PHEV Adds 349-HP AWD Option
7 photos
Photo: Jaecoo / edited
Controlled by Chinese automaker Chery, the Jaecoo brand has expanded the 7 range for the United Kingdom with two Luxury+ configurations. Officially dubbed 7 SHS-P Luxury+, this fellow has a few things going for it, beginning with optional AWD and a larger battery. 349 ponies are on the menu in AWD flavor, and revised driver assistance software also needs highlighting.
Starting with the ADAS part, British media recently put the Hybrid Pure to the test. It recorded six false driver monitoring alerts and two false lane departure warnings on the test route, which is why the Jaecoo finished sixth out of seven participants. Criticized for its sensitivity, the advanced driver assistance suite promises to be less intrusive in the Luxury+.
A new one-touch setting lets British customers apply their preferred assistance configuration without digging through multiple digital menus via the central touchscreen. If you ask me, that's a sensible change to prioritize for the new model year. After all, any type of active automotive safety equipment should make driving easier rather than hinder the experience.
The revised ADAS software is debuting in the Luxury+, yes, but the rest of the 7 will get it from early 2027. Having cleared that up, the plug-in hybrid version of the Super Hybrid System is finally available with all-wheel drive. This powertrain is rated at 354 ps (349 hp), with peak torque estimated at 490 Nm (361 lb-ft).
In optimal conditions, the Luxury+ PHEV AWD needs 5.9 seconds to hit 62 miles per hour (100 kilometers per hour). On paper, that's quite a jump from the 7.9 seconds of the front-drive model. Rated at 204 ps (201 hp) and 365 Nm (269 lb-ft) of twist, said version takes 7.9 seconds and costs £1,500 less.
Photo: Jaecoo The Luxury+ plug-in hybrid with all-wheel drive comes with the usual compromise, namely less electric range than its front-wheel-drive sibling. Jaecoo estimates 70 miles (113 kilometers) on a full charge as opposed to 79 miles (127 kilometers) with front-wheel drive, and that's all due to the additional weight of the electrified rear axle.
In the Luxury+, the high-voltage battery has been upgraded from the former 18.4 kilowatt-hours to 26.6 kilowatt-hours, marking an increase of approximately 45 percent. Jaecoo says the upgrade adds up to 23 miles of electric-only range compared to the current plug-in hybrid system. For customers who do most of their driving around town, said extra capacity will come in handy.
DC fast charging also gets upgraded to 65 kilowatts, with Jaecoo quoting 15 minutes from 30 to 80 percent state of charge. Under the hood, both the front- and all-wheel-drive PHEVs feature a 1.5-liter turbocharged inline-four mill. Beyond pure-electric driving, both switch between series- and parallel-hybrid operation.
The 1.5 underhood is claimed to deliver 44.5 percent thermal efficiency, which is a lot. By comparison, Toyota often claims 40 and 41 percent nowadays for its 2.5- and 1.5-liter hybrid mills. Jaecoo 7 customers who are wondering if the Luxury+ with all-wheel drive can hold its own in off-pavement scenarios will be happy to learn that 183 millimeters (7.2 inches) of ground clearance is the norm.
The approach and departure angles are listed as 20.5 and 28.5 degrees, respectively. While said figures don't threaten the Jeep Wrangler Rubicon, they're good enough for the occasional venture off the beaten path.
As of this writing, Jaecoo's British division lists the 7 SHS-P Luxury+ at £37,000 with front-wheel drive or £38,500 for the all-wheel-drive version. Both are covered by a seven-year vehicle warranty and eight years for the high-voltage battery.

Posted By: Northern Miner Staff November 18, 2026
Copper fell to a seven-month low in London on Wednesday as a stronger dollar and doubts about spending on artificial intelligence weighed on prices even as Chinese smelters face the prospect of paying miners to keep their furnaces fed.
Three-month copper touched $12,700 a tonne and traded at $12,770, down 3.5%, at 6 a.m. Toronto time, Reuters reported. In Shanghai, consultancy CRU expects the 2027 annual treatment charge to settle between minus $50 and minus $100 per tonne of copper concentrate, BMO Capital Markets commodities analysts Helen Amos and George Heppel wrote Wednesday from the World Copper Conference.
Even at the same headline fee, “the reality for smelter economics will vary heavily depending on acid price arrangements, metal payables terms and other commercial terms,” the BMO analysts wrote.
Treatment charges
The two prices measure different things. London futures track refined copper, while the treatment charge is what a miner normally pays a smelter to process concentrate. When smelters compete for scarce feed, the charge can turn negative, giving the miner a premium. A smelter can offset some of the loss by selling sulphuric acid, a by-product, although acid prices have fallen since July, BMO said.
The squeeze is already more severe for smelters buying cargoes on the spot market. Trader-to-smelter treatment charges are below minus $200 per tonne of concentrate. CRU estimates that Chinese smelters’ average cash margin has fallen to nearly minus $200 a tonne from around break-even in July, according to BMO. Chilean miner Antofagasta (LSE: ANTO) is negotiating next year’s terms with Chinese smelters.
Buyers of refined metal in China are also paying more for prompt delivery. The Yangshan premium, paid on top of the London price for imported copper, reached $350 a tonne on Tuesday, up from $290 the day before, Reuters reported. CRU still expects a global refined surplus of about 200,000 tonnes in 2026 and 2027, BMO said. Print

Pebble Makes Things Right After Owners Go Public With Disastrous 1-Year Experience With Pebble Flow
87 photos
Photo: Pebble RV
There are two sides to every story, and Pebble RV, a California-based startup promising "the trailer of tomorrow" with the futuristic, all-electric, self-driving Pebble RV, would like the chance to tell theirs before you make up your mind on the quality of the build of that trailer. They know they messed up, they say.
A story broke last weekend, when Ryan and Celeste, owners of a Pebble Flow travel trailer went on the record with their nightmarish one-year experience. They claimed the trailer was sub-par in terms of quality, construction, and functionality, and that bad customer service delayed their registration of the unit and effectively barred them from using it before it stuff started to fall apart.
It was a damning expose, and the two did on camera for RV consumer advocate Liz Amazing and her YouTube channel, backing their story with photos confirming issues encountered and fails that had appeared on the unit in storage. It was bad enough that all these were happening on a new unit , but it seemed even more so that it happened on a unit they did not use once camping.
Cracked fiberglass, cracked weather seals, a warped rear window, a solar panel lost on the way, a stabilizer foot pad lost the same way, and issues with the charger and the Two Assist system were just some of the issues Ryan and Celeste mentioned.
Photo: Pebble RV At the time the video was published, Pebble was yet to go on the record, even though commenters had already started pestering them with messages urging them to buy back the lemon from the couple.
Pebble RV took its time to respond to Ryan and Celeste's story, but what they say will probably make up for that. They recognize and accept the couple's version of the story, admitting that this first unit "did not meet their expectations or the standards we set for ourselves." They're also saying they have been in touch with the couple and will be buying back the faulty unit .
Pebble also adds some context.
Photo: YouTube/Liz Amazing The company says that, when the video was published, they had resolved all but two warranty repairs reported by the couple, both of which had been reported that same week. They own up to having delayed the registration of the trailer, they apologize for it.
Pebble also says that, earlier in 2026, they voluntarily recalled 22 units of the Pebble Flow after a single report of a detached solar panel, but they don't say whether it was this particular unit . Of these recalled units, 21 have already been repaired and returned, and one is still pending retrieval.
Pebble also mentions that, since the Founders Edition Pebble Flow went into production, which is what Ryan and Celeste bought in November 2025 for $190,000, they have implemented over "300 design and manufacturing improvements" into what is now Gen2 2027 Pebble Flow. The implication seems to be that these erase many of the faults noticed by the couple in their early version .
Photo: YouTube/Liz Amazing "Ryan was candid with me about what went wrong, and I'm grateful for that," Bingrui Yang, Pebble founder and CEO, says in the statement, assuring existing customers and pre-order holders that "we'll keep working until every owner has the experience we set out to build."

Changes to Tesla App and Firmware Show That One of the Most Requested Features Is Finally Coming
6 photos
Photo: @sydney_ev via X
Tesla might be preparing to offer owners the possibility to start battery preconditioning at the press of a button, both in the app and on the vehicle's infotainment screen. Changes to the Tesla firmware and its mobile app have been implemented with the 2026.44 firmware update, as well as the 4.63 Tesla app update. This has been one of the most requested features, especially from customers in less developed markets.
Tesla is well regarded for its software features and quality, and it has a long history of listening to customer requests. That has worked pretty well in the beginning, even though Elon Musk has served as the sole point of contact with the public via social media. However, once Tesla expanded its vehicle lineup and sales, and Musk diverted his attention from Tesla, things got more complicated.
Kudos to the Tesla software team; they have done a great job prioritizing those features that make the most sense for the most Tesla owners. They have also taken steps to simplify Tesla software by removing redundant and least-used functions. However, there are still some features that have been requested for a long time, with no sign that they will ever be offered.
Apple CarPlay support is one of them, even though rumors have continued to float about Tesla finally caving. Many thought the 2025 Holiday Update would include it, but that passed, as well as the Spring Update , Summer Update , and, recently, the Halloween Update , with no result. Probably that's not going to happen, as Tesla's biggest fans insist it doesn't make sense.
Another highly desired feature is manual battery preconditioning. Unlike other carmakers, Tesla has solely relied on an automatic preconditioning function. This triggers after entering a Tesla Supercharger or a supported third-party charging station as a destination in the navigation system.
This works pretty well in markets where the Tesla Supercharger network is well represented. However, once you cross into Eastern Europe, or even further south, in Italy or Greece, Superchargers are few and far between. The problem worsens when there isn't a supported third-party charger in your area, and your Tesla doesn't know that it needs to precondition for DC fast charging.
Well, the good news is that Tesla is finally considering manual preconditioning in upcoming updates. Based on the 2026.44 firmware, Tesla has already added the required software hooks to make this visible to the owners. Corresponding changes have been introduced in the Tesla app with the 4.63 build, so it's fair to expect that you'll also be able to precondition the battery from the phone before even getting into the car.
Although both the firmware and the app have started rolling out to Tesla vehicles worldwide, the feature hasn't been activated yet. It most probably depends on a server-side switch, or other changes that will come with future software iterations. My best prediction is the 2026 Holiday Update, which is expected to be announced in just a couple of weeks. West Coast Customs has finished its first electric Chevy Bel Air, and there’s not much Chevy left under the paint. The Burbank shop cut the body off a Tesla Model 3, kept the entire rolling platform, and set a 1955 Bel Air shell on top of it.
The result, called Project B-Zero, looks like a ’55 Chevy from the curb and like a Model 3 as soon as you open the door. And it charges at Tesla Superchargers.
An old body on a new platform
In the shop’s new video, “The First Ever Electric Bel Air,” founder and CEO Ryan Friedlinghaus explains that a longtime client, Troy Swope, wants to convert an entire car collection to electric and picked the Bel Air to go first. WCC had previously built the same client a Chevelle with a big gas engine.
Friedlinghaus, who drives a Tesla himself, decided against pulling the Model 3’s motors and battery out and fitting them into the old Chevy. Instead, the Tesla stays whole and the Chevy becomes the body kit.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That’s a formula WCC has used for years with gas cars. The shop calls it “old school meets new school”: an old GTO body on a new GTO, an old Camaro on a new Camaro, an old Mustang on a new Mustang. B-Zero is the first time it did it with a Tesla underneath.
Image: West Coast Customs/YouTube
“It sounds easy, but that process was tedious,” Friedlinghaus said.
The wheelbase problem
Before any Chevy sheet metal went on, the crew took the bare Model 3 skateboard for a spin on the streets around the shop, with no doors, no lights and no seatbelts. Friedlinghaus joked about how many safety violations they were racking up. But it drove fine.
Image: West Coast Customs/YouTube
The real headache was the wheelbase. A 1955 Chevy rides on a 115-inch wheelbase, while the Model 3 sits at 113.2 inches. On its gas builds, WCC can cut, shorten or lengthen the newer car’s frame to match the old body. You can’t do that with a Tesla, since the floor is the battery pack.
So the shop changed the body instead, stretching the Bel Air’s rear wheel wells so the wheels sit where they look like they belong.
Bel Air outside, Model 3 inside
The client wanted the exterior to read as a mostly stock Bel Air. The original car was red, so WCC kept it red, with a satin finish and gloss black accents.
Inside, it’s a Model 3. The shop kept the Tesla’s interior, including the steering wheel and center touchscreen, and modified it to fit the Chevy body. The seats got black suede with white stitching in an octagon pattern that Friedlinghaus said was borrowed from the Lamborghini Urus, plus red accents and a “B-Zero” script on the dash.

For many owner-operators, the hardest part of running a truck isn’t driving. It’s everything else: finding steady freight, managing costs, and carving out time for family. Richard Loya Jr., owner of Classic Trucking LLC, has spent the past six years learning all three, and he says the lesson that mattered most was realizing he had stopped being a driver and become a business owner.
Loya recently sat down for a special interview presented by Amazon Relay to talk about what the work looks like from the driver’s seat. He covered his path from warehouse floor to his own authority, how contract freight changed his business, and how he approaches the numbers that decide whether an owner-operator survives.
From the warehouse to the cab
Loya has held his CDL for eight years. Before that, he worked a string of jobs, mostly in warehousing and logistics in Southern California, where he said that kind of work is “what you got to go with.” He spent most of his warehouse career selecting orders, including a stint in the freezer that he admits didn’t suit him. “I’m a tropical person,” he said. “I like the heat.”
He eventually moved into driving for the same company, running deliveries to fast-food restaurants and offloading 48-foot trailers himself. The job also meant key drops, opening stores and shutting off alarms in the early hours. He recalled one 4 a.m. stop in East Los Angeles when the alarm wouldn’t quit and cars began pulling up to watch. It was grueling work, and it came with a schedule that kept him from ordinary life. Working nights and weekends meant he rarely saw daylight and was too tired on Sundays to enjoy his one day off.
Friends who had already made the jump into trucking kept telling him the same thing: if he was going to work that hard, he should do it for himself. When COVID hit in 2020, he was running routes and staying overnight up north, and the logic finally clicked. “If I’m going to be doing all this work, I might as well do it myself,” he said. He saved up, bought a truck, and started his own authority.
Trading brokers for stability
For his first couple of years, Loya hauled through a broker, and he found the arrangement unpredictable. Some weeks there was freight, and some weeks there wasn’t. “You’re doing the hard work, being on time, being safe, doing everything you need to do, and then for them to not at least give you the opportunity to work,” he said. The inconsistency, he added, was “messing up the flow.”
A friend suggested he try Amazon Relay. Once he learned how the platform worked, he said, things improved quickly. The biggest change was a sense of control. “It puts it in my hands,” Loya said. “I’m not relying on a broker to find work. Now it’s all on me. I’m going to rise or fall. It’s my choice, and that’s kind of what I wanted when I bought my own truck.”
His days now are simpler. Much of the work is dropping and hooking trailers, and he can concentrate on being on time and safe. For Loya, that consistency mattered during the freight recession, when many carriers left the industry. “I have always been able to find work with Relay” he said. “There are a lot of people who are just looking for the opportunity to work, and it’s there.”
It has also shaped how he balances work and home, particularly with a two-year-old and a 20-year-old daughter. Loya described two ways to work with Relay. For Loya, contracts offer predictable, recurring freight, while the load board offers flexibility when something comes up with family. “That day I’m not going to take a contract, I’m going to put something on the load board and build my week out however I can make it work,” he said. Some weeks he takes loads that keep him close to home, and others he goes out to earn more. “It’s about finding the balance.”
At Amazon’s RelayCon in Las Vegas, Loya said he took away a simple message about contract freight. “The contracts are really the stability part,” he said. “. If you want to have the consistency, for sure, contracts are right.”
Doing the math on every load
Having freight to haul doesn’t mean every load is a good one, and Loya is blunt about what it takes to stay profitable. He handles permits, insurance, and maintenance himself, and he runs the numbers before accepting a run. Fuel is the largest expense, and he knows California prices are among the highest in the country. To keep that cost down, he uses a fuel card at smaller, more local chains that offer discounts, rather than at the big national stops.
Deadhead miles come first when he evaluates a load. “It’s a big one,” he said. “I have everything pre-factored in my head. When I’m looking at something, I’ve got to know the cost per mile. I do a quick addition of how many miles, and see if it makes sense for me.” He knows his insurance costs, fuel costs, and maintenance costs, and he builds each load decision around them.
He also keeps several mechanics on call, since the best shop is often the busiest one when something breaks. “You gotta have two, three, maybe even four that you can go to if something happens,” he said. The host noted that this is easier to do in a large market like Los Angeles than in more rural parts of the country.
Learning the business side
Loya’s approach to growth is to keep learning from everyone he meets. He treats events like RelayCon as a chance to hear what other owner-operators are dealing with and to take something back to his own operation. “I try to learn a little bit from different people and kind of build my own,” he said.
He applies the same mindset to overhead. When his insurance renews, he calls around to five different providers and asks for a breakdown of the rate. “Sometimes they’ll even go a lot lower, and you don’t even realize it,” he said. “You’re kind of negotiating in a way. They want your business.”
That discipline reflects a distinction, being a good driver and being a good business owner are different skills, and the second doesn’t develop automatically. FreightWaves Editorial Director and former driver, Adam Wingfield said, “You have to be intentional about getting better at business,” noting that an operation that only moves when its owner is behind the wheel is difficult to build on, or to leave to anyone else.
Loya said he feels that gap. “Don’t be so focused on just driving as a job. You’re running the whole business, even if it’s one truck,” he said. “I’ve got to gain the knowledge first.”
Something to leave behind
The knowledge matters because of what Loya wants Classic Trucking to become. He wants to leave the company to both of his daughters. “I wanted it to be something I could leave to both of them and have it established, and they just take over,” he said. “I think they have a leg up on things. I started from scratch.”
He acknowledges he is still working out how to get there, and he doesn’t pretend to have it figured out. But his plan is to keep experimenting, including with other opportunities within Amazon Relay that he hasn’t tried yet. “Don’t be scared to try it out,” he said. “If it doesn’t work, go back to what you know. Sometimes those new opportunities will show you something that works out pretty good.”
His advice for other operators was brief. “Anything worth doing takes time,” Loya said. “It’s not easy all the time, but you’ve got to stick with it.”

Jennifer Ramirez logged more flight time than most owner-operators log windshield time just to sit down for this conversation. She flew from LAX to Dallas-Fort Worth, then on to Chattanooga, Tennessee, for a special report produced with Amazon Relay. The owner-operator behind Harold’s Express Inc., based out of Ontario, California, made the trip to give a carrier’s-eye view of where the freight market stands today, and what it actually takes to keep a family trucking business profitable in 2026.
Harold’s Express Inc. traces back to 1989, when Ramirez’s father first got behind the wheel in Los Angeles. The business he built started in dirt and aggregate hauling, a corner of trucking defined by speed and volume, where success often comes down to who reaches the quarry first and how many loads a truck can turn in a day.
That pace eventually wore on him. Competition among carriers in that niche kept intensifying, Ramirez said, and the constant rushing between sites carried risk. Her father decided he wanted to slow things down, and the company pivoted into dry van freight. He traded the sprint of dirt hauling for a steadier, more measured operation.
Ramirez grew up inside that transition. She was often right alongside her father with grease on her hands, and the career path was never really in question. When classmates were asked what they wanted to be when they grew up, her answer was always, “I want to be a truck driver.” None of her siblings wanted to take over the business, so when the time came, Ramirez stepped in. “This is my time,” she said, “and I’ve been helping him ever since.”
Two decades in, Ramirez has watched the mechanics of booking freight change almost entirely. Where carriers once had to show up in person to secure business, the process now lives on a screen. “Now you do everything from a tablet, phone,” she said, noting that it’s completely different from how the industry used to operate.
That shift cuts both ways for a small carrier. It’s easier for Harold’s Express to be seen by shippers and brokers who would have been out of reach a generation ago. “You have the opportunity to present yourself… to companies or shippers,” as Ramirez put it. It’s easier, in turn, to find work that fits her lanes and equipment without the overhead of constant in-person sales calls.
Technology hasn’t erased the pressures of running a carrier in California, though. The biggest operational headwind facing Harold’s Express today is fuel.
“In California, our fuel is more expensive than other states, and the fuel surcharge base rate is based on a nationwide average,” Ramirez said. The mismatch leaves California-based carriers absorbing a gap between what they pay at the pump and what their surcharge covers. With a fuel-card discount, Ramirez said diesel was running her about $6.99 a gallon; without one, prices in the state can climb past $7.
As long as you book work at a good rate, Ramirez said, the surcharge pressure is manageable. She leans on a short list of tools to protect her margin : pre-planned routes, fuel-card discounts, GPS navigation kept current, and a fleet coached to avoid unnecessary speed.
“Let’s try to keep speed steady,” Ramirez said of the conversations she has with her drivers, “or have a sweet spot when you’re driving, so we’re not burning fuel.”
Discipline shows up in how Ramirez tracks cost per mile. She treats that number with as much attention as any rate confirmation. Chief among her priorities is avoiding deadhead miles, something she called a “lost art” in today’s market.
“I’m really, really big with that,” Ramirez said. “I try to book work where I park,” so she isn’t burning unpaid miles just to reposition between loads.
Ramirez’s approach of booking loads near wherever her trucks are already parked is a direct hedge against the math.
She applies the same scrutiny to maintenance and equipment costs, keeping her trucks running well and staying wary of high payments on newer vehicles. On the revenue side, she chooses to lean on contract work rather than pure spot-market booking to insulate herself from fuel-surcharge swings.
“If fuel charge is going to be very high,” Ramirez said, “I try to book something so that when that price goes up, it’s not going to affect what I have booked.”
Ramirez evaluates loads with patience. She says that there’s often a temptation to rush into booking something, anything, just to keep a truck covered.
Much of that discipline is easier to maintain, Ramirez said, because of how Harold’s Express Inc. uses Amazon Relay . She described the platform as an amazing opportunity built around the things that matter most to a small carrier trying to plan its business, which include visible rates, visible work availability and visible pickup times.
“The transparency with rates… you can see it all,” Ramirez said. “Work availability, pickup times — everything works well for my business.”
The biggest advantage isn’t rate transparency alone. It’s also getting paid on time.
“In order for a business to grow or to be successful,” Ramirez said, “is to work with shippers that pay on time.” She contrasted that with an experience many carriers know well: shippers who promise payment “next week” and then let three weeks pass with nothing in the bank. With Amazon Relay, she said, that hasn’t been an issue. “Weekly payments, invoices on time. It just works amazing.”
She also pointed to responsive Relay carrier support as a reason the relationship works. she said, “so any issues that I have get resolved.”
Ramirez doesn’t define success by fleet size. It’s not how big a business looks from the outside, she said. She’s watched other carriers chase growth for its own sake, booking loads simply to keep drivers working even when the math doesn’t hold up.
“Some carriers are booking loads because they want their drivers to keep working, but they’re not making any profits,” Ramirez said. For Harold’s Express Inc., staying smaller and staying profitable is her biggest concern, though she’s not opposed to scaling up when the opportunity is right.
Consistency plays into that calculus, too. Rather than chasing loads off the open board, Ramirez chooses to book much of Harold’s Express Inc. on contract work with Amazon, which keeps her trucks moving through the slow seasons that typically squeeze smaller carriers. “I stay busy,” she said. “Even in the slow season, I stay busy with Amazon.”
Cost discipline, booking strategy, and her use of Amazon Relay are all in service of something bigger for Ramirez: time with her family. She currently spends four or five days out on the road before heading home for about a week.
Last Thanksgiving, she spent the holiday in her truck.
“Myself, I was sitting in my truck last year for Thanksgiving,” Ramirez said. That experience changed how she planned her year going forward. “Next year, I’m not doing this,” she remembers deciding. “I want to be home.” This year, she’s made good on that promise, making it home for birthdays and other celebrations, with hopes of being home for both Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Heading into peak season, Ramirez said business has stayed strong all year, with the help of her work with Amazon. “It’s been busy already,” she said. “We’ll see what we can do as volumes build.”
The combination of steady work, disciplined cost management and a reliable on-time payments she can count on is what Ramirez sees carrying Harold’s Express Inc. into its next chapter.
